extracted.intended_audience: artists, architects, sculptors, art_historians, and educated readers interested in criticism of Renaissance and monumental art
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative principles and standards for assessing and producing monuments, sculpture, and architecture in the Renaissance/traditional idiom, emphasizing taste, symbolism, originality, and the dangers of formalism and pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatrical, stage-like monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: Monuments and portrait-statues should not present themselves 'like an actor upon a stage' or adopt stage attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes tomb-statues that rise and 'presented itself in front of the tomb, like an actor upon a stage,' surrounded by allegorical figures and theatrical scenery; such presentation induces no memory of death and is symptomatic of frivolous, thoughtless taste. Avoid arranging monuments as theatrical scenes or spectacles seeking applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain allegorical accumulation and pomp
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not surround memorials with an indiscriminate crowd of Fame, Victory, genii, muses, and personifications; avoid symbols of adulation and pomp for their own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author condemns monuments 'surrounded ... by allegorical figures of Fame and Victory, by genii and muses, by personifications of humbled kingdoms and adoring nations' as examples of flattery and insolence. Use allegory sparingly and purposefully; excessive allegorical entourage signals false taste and adulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sober, meaningful symbolism to ornate display
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic elements should be simple, legible, and express genuine theological or moral meanings rather than serve as decorative excess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By contrast with theatrical tombs, the author praises a simple sarcophagus with 'censers attached to crosses; a most beautiful symbolic expression of Christ's mediatorial function' and a wreath of vine leaves. Favor solemn, symbolic expression over ornamented crowding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject vanity and self-glorifying inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Epitaphs and inscriptions must avoid boastful, presumptuous language that claims reward or elevates earthly nobility above spiritual humility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Pesaro epitaph, which 'expects the noblest crown' and claims family nobility 'only a little lower than that of the angels,' is singled out as example of classicizing carnal pride. Inscriptions should not read as claims to deserved heavenly reward or as inflated social self-regard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid grotesque, tasteless sculptural motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not employ demeaning or grotesque figures, clownish caryatides, or incoherent combinations of forms that produce horror or ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Doge John Pesaro monument is criticized for 'four colossal negro caryatides, grinning and horrible' and other monstrous adjuncts; such grotesquerie reflects base feeling and degraded taste. Sculpture should preserve dignity, proportion, and humane expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should be original, not mere copy or rule-following
rubrics_metrics.description: Good work is 'not a copy, nor anything done by rule, but a freshly and divinely imagined thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues repeatedly that if a work is truly good it cannot be produced by rote adherence to precepts (e.g., Vitruvian orders); originality and imaginative invention are the hallmarks of noble art. Discard slavish imitation of classical formulas when seeking true artistic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat codified rules as aids for beginners, not ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Written laws, explicit rules, and formal systems are useful for novices but inadequate for the mature artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements like 'all written or writable law respecting the arts is for the childish and ignorant' and 'there are more laws perceived and fulfilled in the single stroke of a great workman, than could be written in a volume' stress that rules teach basics but cannot create great art. Beware artists who boast of living 'by the law'—this indicates lack of true genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject mechanized/formulaic production in architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture should not be reduced to machine-produced application of fixed orders and proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that if the five orders are fixed proportions, machines could be set to cut pillars and friezes and 'we may dispense with our architects altogether.' Such mechanization signals the loss of architectural artistry; architecture must remain inventive and responsive to human imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value expressive invention over formal 'orders'
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural beauty arises from inventive design, not adherence to a small set of canonical orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He contends 'Five orders! There is not a side chapel in any Gothic cathedral but it has fifty orders' and that inventive souls can create countless new forms. Therefore, the system of orders and proportion should be subordinated or rejected in favor of creative invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let intellectual formalism (philology/logic/rhetoric) supplant substance
rubrics_metrics.description: An excessive focus on words, grammar, logic, and rhetorical form produces shallowness and dishonesty in artists and scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The renewal of pagan study led to absorption in 'grammar, logic, and rhetoric,' making 'men shallow and dishonest.' The guidance is to prioritize the substance, feeling, and inner truth of work over pedantic concerns with form or stylistic pyrotechnics that conceal lack of depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against pride (state, knowledge, system) as corrupting force
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride—whether pride of state, knowledge, or system—corrupts art, producing vanity, formalism, and the degradation of true feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the passage the author names three elements—Pride of State, Pride of Knowledge, Pride of System—that drove Renaissance corruption. He contrasts law 'written upon the heart' with prideful lettered law and insists that pride turns obedience to law into hypocrisy. Artists should cultivate humility and an obedience to the 'spirit' rather than proud compliance with externals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor inspiration and tacit skill over explicit teachable formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: Great workmanship is guided by an inexpressible, divinely-taught subtle science that cannot be fully communicated by rules or manuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lines such as 'His science is inexpressibly subtle, directly taught him by his Maker, not in any wise communicable or imitable' and 'there are no laws by which we can write Iliads' indicate that masters are guided by inner inspiration and experience; teaching should aim to foster insight, not to substitute formulas for genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the proper role of law: correction for the childish, not replacement of conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rules and written laws are necessary to restrain sin and guide the simple, but they must not supplant higher, heartfelt obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author distinguishes 'the law of the letter' (which 'killeth') from 'the law of the Spirit' (which 'giveth life'). For artistic practice, external prescriptions help novices, but moral and aesthetic life require internalized, humble conformity to higher principles rather than proud literalism.
